newsitem.title: USA: Passenger carriers must improve cargo operations.
newsitem.headline: Passenger carriers must improve cargo operations.

text.p: The world's major airlines urgently need to reform their cargo divisions dropping habits that make them uncompetitive with integrators like Federal Express, said Dublin based industry consultant John Harnett.
Otherwise they could be left with as little as 30 percent of the international freight market by 2013, with the integrators holding the lion's share reversing the current market spilt.

Until Sunday, Harnett headed airline interest group Cargo Media, which had studied ways to speed automation. It has now been succeeded by Cargo 2000, a new IATA group of airlines and forwarders with a broader mandate to identify reform measures.

This challenge facing Cargo 2000 was underlined by Harnett at a workshop at IATA Cargo Week 97, who criticized the traditional passenger/cargo carrier industry as hidebound, inefficient and excessively process oriented.
Forwarders and airlines have not tackled the real issues, which are to cut redundant processes and costs whilst improving service. Only recently have they recognized the need for change, he said.

A recent Unisys survey showing the average international air freight movement on scheduled carriers takes six full days, from door to door, or just six hours less than it did in 1975. IATA found that 78 percent of that time, freight sits in warehouses.

Warehousing, said Harnett, is a major additional cost, particularly at a major airport. Unisys found that of the total time a shipment is in the airline's hands, less than 10 percent of it is spent flying.

This Unisys survey found that a normal freight shipment in 1996 involved an average of 40 processes, covering the actual movement of the goods and the supporting paperwork. A comparable shipment performed by an integrated carrier involves 11 processes.
The extra 29 processes employed by the airlines "disimprove service to the customer and add cost," he said.
Each piece of freight was handled an average of 36 times. It was counted or checked, on average, 16 times, and stored in eight different locations and generated 12 pieces of paper, he said.
Harnett said the survey demonstrated that the traditional air freight stream is unreliable because of poor and fragmented processes and the absence of standards, measurements and controls.
Airlines which are making public their performance statistics are not giving the customer much relevant information, although the information is highly relevant to the airlines.

Viewing massive investment in EDI technology by forwarders and airlines should not be seen as a panacea and would not make the scheduled cargo stream more efficient unless first there is a great deal of process reform to cut shipment time and cost, Harnett said.

For years, the airline and freight forwarders were lulled into complacency by forecasts from trade associations and aircraft manufacturers suggesting that global air freight would grow at an annual 6.5 to 8.5 percent.
Total air freight traffic has been rising by as much as seven percent per annum, but share of the market for scheduled air freight business is declining, he noted.
And while the yields of combination carriers are falling, the reason is not excess capacity but rather the steady loss of higher yielding cargo to the integrated carriers, Harnett stated.
